Oh, sure. Papatio was a nice musician. Papatio, George Field, you know, nice musicians. And Perez, Anah Mettoyer.
How do you spell that name, Norman? Who's that? The trumpet player.
Anah. Mettoyer.
That's M-E-T-O-Y-E-R.
That's it? Correct. That gets it. Mettoyer.
Well, one other question, and there'll be a few in a minute here, unless you want to stop right now.
Now you say Mettoyer in French. Mettoyer. Mettoyer, yeah. Mettoyer.
What was his first name? Armand?
Anah. Anah. A-N-O-R-L-D. Anah.
I see. One other question. Mettoyer, did you tell me you played with Bolden sometimes, do you? When you were very young, you played with Bolden?

Well, after Frank, long after, I played with Frank. Frank had a band. It was gone. Frank had changed his band name. It's called his band name, The Eagle Band. Well, he had Buddy. Played with Buddy on his job. I said Elizabeth Hall. Frank had a Masonic Hall every Saturday night. That was Rampart and Padilla. Frank had a Masonic Hall. He was blown, but going off. That play, he wouldn't stop sometimes. Then Frank leaves him going. He got sick then. That's why they kept him home. They just sent him out and all the tensed of them. Then Frank taking a fellow they called Edouard Clem. He was a one-eyed fellow. He was from a reserve of the country. Then Edouard played with Frank. Frank leaves Edouard go. Joe used to come around on Saturday night. Joe was working Butler for White people out front of town, but always studying music. Joe would come around on a Saturday night dressed up and always treat the band. He'd treat the fellas. Treat Frank, you know. And Frank would leave him play a number. Was he very good then? Could Joe play trumpet all right? Yeah, Joe could play pretty good. He was strong. And he could read. That's what Frank liked it. So Frank taking him in the band. You mean instead of Bolden? Oh, Bolden, that's after Bolden. After Bolden. After Bolden, yeah. After Bolden. After Bolden, yeah.
I was wondering about Carnish. When he stopped playing with Bolden, did he stop playing music, or did he keep on playing after that? Willie Carnish on trombone. Did he keep on working around here?
Yeah, a couple of them should play sometimes. He played with the Little Tuxedo Brass Band. He kept on working. Yeah, he'd play in the Brass Band like that. And catch a job like that he'd play.

Who was the first one really to play the slide trombone, as you say? Your uncle was the first one to do? My uncle. Doce Bonetta. Before that, they used mostly vowels. Vowels, that's all. When you were playing with Ori, was he playing slide or valve? Who? Kid Ori. Was that the other way? Ori always did use the slide, didn't he?
Ori? Yes. Yeah, Ori always did use the slide, since I started with Ori.
You think a lot later, of course, than Doceman.

Yeah, Ori always used the slide, since I knew him. I played with him. Well, slide was favorite then. It was all the vowels that was going out of style. Because Frank, he was never much on a slide. Well, Ori had a pretty good year for music. That's why Joe liked him so much. Catch on pretty quick. No, pretty quick. Also, Johnny. Johnny would catch on, make things, various from a violin like that, like piano and things like that. Johnny would catch it. He'd just bust out a laugh when he'd make it. And so, I went off to violins. We gave a job to a fellow, a band. Well, he was using seven pieces, you see. Give a job to a fellow. Joe did. And he went and played a job with six pieces. Well, when they hired Joe again, he says, listen, we're going to hire the band, but he says, how can't we have six pieces? We can't hear the violin much. So, this went on like that. So, this went on like that. When he said that, I quiff. Yeah, I quiff. So, when I quiff, he goes and get Barty Biggar's uncle, Emil, Biggar, to play a father. When I hear that rumor, I say, yeah, well, I'll get on the violinist for a stand. See, one band with me started the business off with six pieces. And the other fellow said, gee, that band sounds pretty good. Well, they wanted everybody to follow suit then. Joe and them hated that because they wanted me all the time. Because when they get a little tangled up with his music, I could show them his division all the time. Tell me, sir. And when they get on the piano or something, after Dixieland Jazz Band came up, using five pieces and things, well, Joe and Ori, they got crazy about that. They wanted to organize on that and follow the style of the Dixieland Band. And they hated to lose me because I could play the piano, too. But I did leave them from the violin.
Excuse me, sir. Do you have a question? I've got to run across the street and make a phone call.
Yeah, well, I think I'll have to continue to run myself, Mr. Bill. Yes. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you.

. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . Yes, sir. What was the name of that? . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . When did you first hear that number? Is that a new number or more? It's about 1935 or something. Why sure. Have you ever played it down here before? I mean some parts of it. Why sure. You know the feature of that? That was Glenn Miller's. You learned that off the record or something? You heard them playing? Oh yeah.

Glenn Miller. Now you take Martha Bobcats. Martha Bobcats is a feature of Bob. Bob Crosby. And Boogie Woogie. Pine Top Smith. Featured by Tommy Dawson. I have to play Boogie was out. He played it good too.

Did you ever hear George Thomas play any of that kind of blues? Somebody told me, I believe Clarence Williams once told me that George Thomas was the first one he heard play that Boogie bass. You remember George Thomas of course. Oh yeah, I remember George Thomas piano player. Yes, played in the district. I think he had made that New Orleans. New Orleans. New Orleans. New Orleans. New Orleans.
New Orleans hopscotch blues. New Orleans hopscotch blues. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Did he play that type of bass sometimes, like the Pine Top bass or any of those Boogie Woogie basses? Did he use that style?

Well, in fact, I never noticed him playing the style of Boogie Woogie. Boogie Woogie is really originally run by a fella that they called him Burmanham. And during the time, there was good friends Burmanham, Jell-O-Roll, and they hired Black Peaks. Well, the fellas used to play blues. Now the first really the top originator of Boogie Woogie that I ever know of, the first one. But he left here. Then he went to Scarborough. Oh, he was a big man. And there was Albert Ambers. Albert Ambers? Ambers. Ambers. Ambers.

Ambers. You remember when he died? Remember when he died, you told me you met him up on Beale Street once, huh? Is that the same fella? I came over and told you about him dying. You said you met him on Beale Street once. Is that the same fella? When I was taking lessons from you. No. What did it take for?
No, that was because Albert died around about four years ago.

Yeah, well that's when I was taking lessons from you. Huh? Albert Ambers, yeah. It never been. Mm-hmm. Because I remember I told you about it and you mentioned knowing. That's all these features of Boogie Woogie. Where did he get that left hand from? Did he invent it himself? Sure. He did. Okay. I'd like to know what Berman Ham played like. Could we get a little recording of that, Bill? Do you think that would be good? Yeah, I'd like to know what Berman Ham played. I don't know.

I don't know. The blues players played them. I don't know. Really come down as blues, but they're basses. Yeah. My left hand was all the way boom, ba-boom, ba-boom, ba-boom, ba-boom, ba-boom, ba-boom, ba-boom, ba-boom, ba-boom, ba-boom, ba-boom, ba-boom, ba-boom, ba-boom, ba-boom, ba-boom,
ba-boom, ba-boom, ba-boom, ba-boom, ba-boom, ba-boom, ba-boom, ba-boom, ba-boom, ba-boom, ba-boom. I wonder where he was from.
Okay, Mr. Mineta, anytime you want to tell us about your life. Oh, gee. Oh, that's something.

Where were you born? Professor? Huh? Where were you born? I'm born in Algea. In Algea. In Algea. In Algea. In Algea. In Algea. In Algea. Want to know my boy? Yes, birthday. Yes, birthday. Well, my own Algea, Louisiana. Third day of October, 1889.
Who were some of your family? Were any of your family interested in music?

Oh, yes. My uncles, Jules and Melinda, and Dues. They were the professionals of the town. What did they play? Well, Jules and Melinda, he was a trumpet player. Well, during that time, they didn't say trumpet, it was cornich, you know. He was a cornich player. Brass, band, and orchestra. And my other uncle, he was a trombonist. He came from Canceritory, from France, down here. And he was the first man that ever known at Oak Steen with a sliding trombone.
You mean they were all the valve trombones before that?

Well, that's all they used to use, valve trombones. That was all the style of valve trombones. But he was the first one for the same. Okay. Jules had a nickname. Yes, he had a nickname. They called him Norm. Norm Manetta.
Norm? Norm, yeah. That's why I was wondering if that was the same man he mentioned. Well, that's it. What did you play your first job with?
My first job, speaking about job, playing out. My first job I played out, I remember, with the old man Tom Albert.
When would that have been about?
It had been around about 19, 19, 19, 19, 19, 19, 19, 19, 19,
19, 19, 19, 19, 19, 19, 19. What instrument were you playing?
I played violin. Violin. Violin.
Was that the first instrument you learned? That's my first instrument.
What was the job? The job was on the, it was on a pleasure boat on the Mississippi River. Excursion? Yeah, pleasure boat ran from, say, Esplanade Street down Chalamet. Down below.
Yeah. What kind of a band did they have? Is it a full six or seven piece band or just a small group?
No, it had violin, outlet violin. He was playing cornette, a guitar, a guitar, a guitar, a guitar, and bass.
When did you take up the piano? Well, I'd taken piano.
After violin, my sister was a pianist. And got disgust of it, a war ration from my mother, helping my mother out. And piano laid up, so my brother put me on the piano.
Who was teaching you piano?

Well, my first teacher was a lady by the name of Miss Laura Albert. She'd go around visiting houses teaching on Tuesdays and Fridays. And then, from my violin, I played for her, and she put on a concert. So the concert formed at Western Chapel's church. That's up on Liberty, between Adila and Saratoga. And I played, my first number was Waves of the Danube Walls, which is now Al Jolson taking it, and made an anniversary song.
Was the whole program classical music in this concert? Oh yeah.
All classical music.
One of the, who else was there for the concert? I don't know about that. Just the two of you.
Well, I played in Miss Albert. She played the piano component, you see.
When did you start working in Storyville? When did you begin playing piano over there? Had you played other places before you went to Lula White's? Oh, sure.

You see, a letter band, Jack Carey's Orchestra, called Crescent Orchestra. Do you want to know the name of the man? Yes, if you can remember. Well, the band, the name of the men, the band. Jack Carey, he was manager. Oscar Silvestre, was cornetist. Old man Willie Umfrey was clarinet. Bebe Mathews was drummer. That's Bill Mathews' brother. He's dead now. He died. Jimmy Johnson was bass violin player. And Charlie Moore was guitar player.
What's his last name?
Charlie Moore. M.W.R.E. Moore. Well, that was the consist of the Crescent Orchestra.
What kind of jobs did they play?
Oh, well, they played dance halls, played picnics, out at Lake Picnics, you know, Sundays, during the week times, house dances.
Well, tell us about these picnics. I never did go to hardly any picnics. And they were out at the lake or her.
Oh, yeah, out at the lake. Gee, uh.
Near Millenburg or West End? Yeah, out Millenburg.
Out West End. Could you describe a picnic to us? Could you describe a picnic scene?
Because I danced. Oh, yeah. You see the picnics. After we had entered the train at Esplanade Street. Go out. Go out to the pavilion.
It was out.
Fully about a block.

Then the, uh, the, uh, what do you call it? The, uh, the, uh, the, uh, the, uh, the, uh, the, uh, the, uh, the, uh, the, uh, the, uh, little pavilion. Yes, little pavilion and the band would play in there. See, they had each side gallery, they danced on the gallery. We played from nine.
Nine in the morning? Nine in the morning. Yes.
And we'd knock off recess at twelve. They had an hour recess while they'd eat. Then we'd come back and we'd eat lunch. And we'd start from about, say, about one to six.
Who would promote these picnics?
Oh, well, they had different clubs.
Clubs?
Right, different clubs.
Now, would a pavilion like that look like Mamalu's, or would it be different?
Well, it would be like on the order of Mamalu's, on that order. Set out on the water. Oh, gee, they had dozens of them.
But didn't you play outdoors, too? Didn't you play outdoors, also? Like on the lawn? You mean on picnic grounds? Yes, picnic grounds.
Oh, yes, I have played. I have played picnic grounds. Like out, uh, Millenburg. Basket picnic, you know what I'm saying?
Yep, everybody brought his own basket.
Yeah, brought their baskets.
What did they serve there? Did they have drinks and so on? Oh, yeah, beer.
Or did you bring your own? No, I guess they brought their little stuff. You know what I mean? But they'd have beer and soft drinks.
At the grounds.
Yeah. But then each one would carry their baskets.
For lunch.

That's right. Now, we play another place, very regular. It was a place called Eastman Farm. They give a lot of picnics. Every Sunday, we'd hire different bands. Where was that? That was back of Carlton.
Is that existing today or the high of the world? No, it's not.

Oh, no. Oh, no. So, from Jack Kerris, we were playing once, an advertisement on a Sunday, for a dance over in Gretna, while we'd play mostly every Sunday night, called the Come Clean. We'd make an advertisement on Sunday. On the wagon. On Monday. Yeah, on the wagon. So, I remember one Sunday, on the corner of 8th and Howard, a gentleman called me out the wagon. Which, he lived on 8th Street. It was a row. And he lived in one of the rows. His name was Ike Jackson. Bass violin player. Oh, he played for Tom Anderson for years. So, playing on the corner, like the bands in their play, he called me off the truck and asked who I was, you see. After I explained who I was, why he had played with my uncles. He had visited the house and everything when I was a small boy. Son asked me, how would I like a job in the district? That was on the corner of Murray and Iberville. It was a saloon. Mac Ischus. The proprietor.
What is the last name? Mac?
Mac Ischus.
Mac Ischus.

Yeah, he is the proprietor of it. It used three pieces in there. He had a mandolin player with him. He had a guitar and he was playing bass. And so, he liked my violin playing. And he asked me, would I accept, would like a job, playing every night? So, after he knew my people, I told him, well, it felt good to me. I was still attending school, the Young University, during that time. So, that went up on St. Charles? Well, St. Charles, no, but they sold it. They sold it and renamed it the Gilbert's Academy. And from Gilbert's Academy, it was sold again. That's Leon Teen and Pitt. Leon Teen and St. Charles Avenue.
How old would you have been then?
Huh?
How old were you then? How old were you?
About 40.
One other question to interrupt. Come Clean Hall, was that across the river or over here?
That was across the river in Gretna.
Was it usual to come here to advertise a dance that took place in Gretna? Did you get offered?
Well, you see, Jack Carey, he was well-liked on this side of the river, and he'd draw the crowd.
He'd draw across the river.
He made our biggest advertising in New Orleans.
I see.
Well, we'd make about five or six blocks in Gretna.

Well, I guess there were signs on the side of the wagon. Oh, sure. That's right. What would it say, for example? I mean, how would it read, you know, for that dance, you know? What would the sign say?

Well, sign would say, on Monday, the date, dance given by the Wolves Club. They had a Wolves Forest Club over the river. Oh, yeah. Which they had a hall, too. They called a Wolves Forest. But these boys, they would throw a dance often at the Come Clean Hall. I see. Was that hand-painted design or printed or? Oh, yeah, hand-painted. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Crescent. Jack Carrier's Crescent Orchestra. Jack Carrier's Crescent Orchestra. Jack Carrier's Crescent Orchestra. Yeah. How much did they charge for those dances? They have the price on them, too, I guess?
Oh, them prices. They're doing them things. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
rent of furniture wagon, you see. Pretty big wagon. Yeah. Have low sides or would it have gates?
No, it had sides and it had a tailgate.
The top on it or was it out where you were sitting in the open?
No, some would have tops and some was open.
Do they look anything like these vegetable wagons you see today? Bigger? Or larger. Or larger. With the same shape?
Same shape.
What did you sit on there? Were the benches on the sides?
No, we had little falling chairs, little round seats, falling chairs.
When you sat there were you facing each other or were you playing? Oh yeah. Yeah, we were fair. How was the benches? That's all I'd like to know.
All right. There's a drummer. He was set right behind the driver. Yeah.
Facing the rear.
Yeah, facing. You know. Facing toward the back of the wagon.
Yeah, by the way.
And the trumpet would be opposite him. Trumpet and trombone side each other. Mm-hmm.
Facing each other. Yeah.
And on this side, well, clarinet would be on my left side, on the right side, with violin.
You'd be sitting along one side of the wagon and there on the other one on the other side? That's right.
And the trombone player, he'd be sitting in the rear with the bass violin player. See where he could use his slides.
Yeah, he'd be facing out the back of the wagon there. Yeah. Where would Charlie Moore be sitting?
Charlie Moore be sitting next to me.
Oh.
Right next to me. Right next to me, he'd be sitting in the bass violin player, right on this side, the drum one player on that side.
The bass, was the bass player looking towards, facing the drummer, is that right? The bass player?
Yeah, the bass player faced the drummer. From the other side?
Yeah, that's it. Yeah. Did you have the trombone next to him?
That's right.
What about other people on the wagon? Would the kids climb on like they do today? Oh, no, indeed.
No, indeed. That wagon was, really consists of about seven pieces.
You didn't have any dancers or singers or nobody like that?
No, no.
Just, and a driver maybe?
Maybe we'd have a fella up with the driver. He'd be hollering out, announcing out to the people, you know. And then, we'd have about three or four boys carrying dodges. Oh, man. You know what?
Carrying what? Notices, like, huh? Oh, yeah. Notices, yeah. Oh, yeah. Yeah.
Each one would have a bum like that. Were they walking around?
Yeah, they'd follow.
They'd follow.
I see. Hand them off to the crowd.

Yeah, you see, like, we'd stop on corners where it was business corners, like saloons. We'd stop, you know, and play. That crowd, and they could see what's going on. Now, sometime we'd ride, about two blocks or three blocks before we'd hit another solo. Well, them boys, they'd distribute bills all in residence. While you were moving from one to another.
Yeah. Would you play while you were moving from one place to another? Oh, no. Not play? No, we'd play right on the corner. You only played when the wagon stopped? Yeah, when the wagon stopped.
What about the people? What were they doing when you stopped?
Were they listening to have to see?

Oh, see, the people, when we stopped, they was near where we stopped at. They'd get to run out their houses there, get on the street, and started dancing, and all the fellas out the saloon, and it sounded so good to some of them guys in the saloon, and say, come on band, play another one, come on out and get a drink. They'd go out, get a drink, then they'd play another number for them. Like that.
Didn't any of the musicians drink?
Huh?
Didn't any of the musicians drink? All of them drank.
All of them drank I knew of.
At the hall that you were speaking of, you know, that you were advertising with the Crescent Band, what did they serve there to drink?
Oh, well, they had, during that time they had, they sell their beer by the Cakes, Cakes beer. Oh, they had all kinds of whiskey, gin, everything.
Did they sell it by the glass? Oh yeah, by the glass. What kind of glasses?

Oh, the beer was a small little bit of glass like that. A little small, I don't know what you'd call that kind of glass. Regular tunk? A little handle on it, but a small glass. Oh yeah, it had a handle on it. So it's fine. Yeah, that's it. How much a glass?
Huh? How much a glass?
Ten cents a glass.
Did they have barrels in those places? Sure. Other than the beer kegs?
Sure.
Beer out of barrels. And what else would they have in the barrels?
Well?
Just beer, would it be wine or what?
Well, no, mostly beer in the barrels, but they had wines there, and they're wine by Quartz. Wines and the whiskeys and all like gills and things.
When you went out to advertise, did you sometimes meet other bands on wagons?
Oh, sure. Sure, we used to buck, we'd call that bucking. We'd say we'd stop this corner, and the fellow would say, Well, there's a kid right there at the next corner.
You'd run?
Well, we'd make a round. Say, let's go get him. They'd come around, a couple of blouse come around, and backbomb, you know. And we'd hit about our best, and it hit their best. And pull off.
Did you both play at the same time, or one and then? No, no, uh-uh.
One band would play. One at a time?
Yeah. And then the other one? That's right.
You wouldn't play at the same time?
No, no, oh no. Did they tie the wheels together sometimes? Of the two wagons? No.
Oh, no.

Sometimes people told us they'd tie the two wagons together so the other band couldn't get away. Couldn't get away. Oh, well. You don't remember that. Matt Carey told me that. What? Matt Carey told me that. He said sometimes they would tie the wagons, and everybody was scared of Kepard, he said. So whatever Kepard's band would, anybody that Kepard would play with would come, they would tie it so that the other band could make a getaway, you know?
That was Freddie Kepard. Yeah. That was Olympia. Olympia band. Mm-hmm.
Well when one band played against the other, then how would you tell who won that contest?
Well, it was left to the majority of people, you know. Was it by applause?
Yeah. Exciting?
That's it, excitement and applause. That's right.
Would the people say anything to you? Huh? Would the people say anything at the end of a number?
Well.
They would come up and tell you?
I'd say, well, they had some people in different parts of the town had their preference.
You mean sometimes we're poor? All bands. More popular in certain sections.

That's right. That's right. Now Uptown, Jack Carrey had it Uptown. Everybody's for Jack. You come downtown, well everybody's for Olympia, the Imperial, or Superior. That's downtown. You usually played with Jack Carrey then.
Did you play many wagon jobs with other bands sometimes? Oh yes. Just anyone that would happen to play?

Yes, I played, I'll tell you, the scene on the job, I played at Arborville. Oh yes, you were. Well it happened once the Shriners came to town. I had two bartenders at McIshies. I had a day bartender and a night bartender. Well, the night bartender, him and his lady friend, they were live parties. They'd go out shopping and they'd stop in the 10 cent store. During that time the Shriners was here and the pop, the piece of the Shriners was a long way to Tipperary and people was buying them songs, man, like hotcakes. So, it was the bartender, Johnny Rice was his name. And his lady friend. Well they bought a copy. Well in that saloon, they had a pianola. But it was always kept locked. Well, on a Monday night, Johnny Rice and his lady friend, they went out shopping, bought a song, they came down that night. And he asked the bass player, say, Ike. We is out today, say, here's the pop, the song, the Shriners, a long way to Tipperary. Well, the man of the player they had, he was an air player. They'd play their own stuff with their hair and things. So, on that time I was there, Ike told him, say, well listen, our violin player will play that for you. If you open that piano. So, he got the key and you open that piano. And, uh, just a little, just like you come off the street in here. And I started playing it. And the Shriners started piling in there, plus all the shipments, you know. And it got packed. And they were throwing dollars around there that night, like shims. And I didn't have to touch my violin at all. I put it in the case and just proceed all that night on the piano. So, he drove, Mr. Lula's old man. He started to crowd raise, stand around. So, he got in the midst, they called me outside. We used to wear, had a locker, go there, and you got a dress coat on, put a little white coat on. So. What kind of white coat?
What did you wear exactly? What did you wear? Huh? What did you wear exactly?
We'd have a white jacket on.
Like a dinner jacket? Or a waiter's jacket? Or a...
Just a little white coat.
Or a little white coat.
Or a little white coat. Or a little white coat. Like a summer coat.
Yeah, like a summer coat.
What kind of trousers? Well, I wore trousers, but we... Well, whatever you had.
What we had on. I see.
Only we just changed our dress coat, you see.
Did you wear a tie? Oh, yeah. Big tie?
Yeah. We wear, we wear a tie. We just took our coat on, you know. A little white coat on. So he says, well listen. He liked it in my playing.

So he said, how would you like to play a job, play in the parlor? He said, you wouldn't wear no white coat, you could stay dressed. Well, no one's at the house, at your leisure, you can go back in the set room and read magazines. You can step out to the corner, it'll give you a buzz when comfort comes.
Who hung in the 25s? Who would be there? Who would hang out in the 25s? Other than musicians and women and men?
Well, that's the only ones that rank around that kind of place because the people that men with respect wouldn't go in them kind of places. They have their own places.
What about Wills? Would he go in the place?

Well, Harry Wills, sure he went in a place like that because the manager of the place was Arnold Doofusho that put up a lot of money on Harry Wills. And he was manager of the place. It was Lala's photo, John Lala's place. But Arnold Doofusho was the manager of it.
Do you know anything about the relationship between John Lala and Pete Lala? Were they?

No, no relation. There were no relations. No. Now listen, Pete Lala's name, he was not Pete Lala. It was Pete Sika Sika. But he just gave him that name, Pete Lala. Pete Lala, I think he was a relative of the trumpet player. Who? Johnny Lala was it?
Well, there's several of them. There's three Mike Lala's. I know three Mike Lala's. Tell about Tom Anderson. Tell now, tell us about Tom Anderson. What's that for you? Well...

Mr. Tom Anderson sent for me. His... My wife's... ...lady friend, I'll say. ...was Gertrude Dix. She ran... The house was called a brass railing. It was right next... ...to Mr. Anderson's Annex Saloon. Mr. Anderson's Annex Saloon. And, uh... I went to wake over there for her. Miss Dix. Well, I played there... ...about... ...or around about... ...eight or nine months.
How old were you by then? About...
